games.canonical_title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas - The Definitive Edition

sections.name: King Dodongo
sections.card: Weak point: tail when he rolls. Toss bombs into his mouth when he inhales. Stay near the arena edge and roll through fire breath.

sections.name: Water Temple
sections.card: Raise/low water with Iron Boots and Longshot. Map the central pillar first; note which gates need water level changes.

sections.name: Glyphid Dreadnought
sections.card: Kite between waves; focus weak-point armor plates as they open. Save overclock/nuke for armor break windows.

sections.name: Hollow Bough
sections.card: Sticky webs and reduced visibility — mobility build or clear web shooters first. XP magnet perks help swarm waves.

sections.name: Tank
sections.card: The big one, the one throwing chunks of concrete at you. While he is up the director stops sending commons and specials outside finales, so it is four guns against one target — but slip past him and the horde comes straight back. Fight him in the open: anything he can punch becomes a projectile with more reach than his fists, and a punch taken near a drop kills rather than knocks down. If the route makes him crouch through a vent he is barely mobile, and he never looks for another way round.

sections.name: The Parish
sections.card: Hold choke points with shotguns; watch rooftop crescendo timing. Medkits before the finale wave.

sections.name: Mind Flayer
sections.card: Break concentration and interrupt psychic links. Position to avoid AoE after each phase shift.

sections.name: Goblin Camp
sections.card: Use elevation and stealth for surprise rounds. Short rest before multi-wave camp defense.

sections.name: Deathclaw
sections.card: Very high health for its level and resistant to nearly everything, energy weapons worst of all — lasers can reflect straight off the hide. It opens with a roar and a ground stomp, headbutts to stagger, and throws cars at you once you are out of reach. Below a certain health it can kill you outright with a grab or a decapitation, and at low level that threshold is higher than it sounds, so distance and cover matter more than raw damage.

sections.name: Corvega Factory
sections.card: Clear raiders floor-by-floor; grenades for clustered groups. Save ammo for Assaultron encounter.

sections.name: Downtown
sections.card: PCSX2: stable 60 FPS needs aggressive EE/IOP tuning. EmuDeck preset recommended for Deck.

sections.name: Final Confrontation
sections.card: Stock riot gear pickups; keep crowd control weapons for riot phases.

sections.name: Megara
sections.card: Learn dash patterns; punish recovery windows. Mirror and trap boons help burst phases.

sections.name: Temple of Styx
sections.card: Buy charms before entry; poison resistance or healing crucial. Route choice affects shop access.

sections.name: Adam Smasher
sections.card: Sandevistan or high DPS builds; destroy legs first. Cover during rocket barrages.

sections.name: All Foods Plant
sections.card: Stealth route saves ammo; quickhack turrets when detected. Deck: lower crowd density settings help FPS.

sections.name: Big Smoke
sections.card: Keep distance during chase; aim for vehicle weak points. Motorcycle section: avoid collisions.

sections.name: Los Santos
sections.card: DE edition: verify Proton forced; shader cache regen after updates. Driving missions: cap FPS for stability.

sections.name: Starter Lot
sections.card: Build small starter home first; career goals unlock skills. Deck: lower sim speed in crowded lots.

sections.name: Get a Job
sections.card: Complete daily tasks for steady income before expanding house. Save before major lot changes.

sections.name: Bear
sections.card: Dead Eye on entry; headshots during slow. Use cover trees; horse keeps distance.

sections.name: Valentine
sections.card: Honor missions affect town mood. Stable upkeep and camp supplies before long hunts.

sections.name: Gels
sections.card: Three paints, all useless on glass. Blue bounces you higher the further you fell. Orange removes friction so you keep whatever speed you arrive with. White lets you portal a surface that refused portals before, but it will not stick to cubes or turrets, and the cleansing spray strips it.

sections.name: Repulsion Gel
sections.card: The blue one. Bounce height scales with how far you dropped, so gain height by falling onto it from somewhere higher, not by jumping. Two coated surfaces facing each other let you climb by bouncing between them.

sections.name: Aerial Faith Plate
sections.card: Launches to a fixed destination, but it keeps the speed you arrive with — so run or fall into one to travel further than it looks. It throws objects as well as you, and its arc can be fed through a portal.

sections.name: Hard Light Bridge
sections.card: Solid light that runs until something blocks it. Put a portal in its path to move the whole bridge somewhere else — it leaves the portal square-on, so centre the portal on the beam. It is also cover: a turret cannot see through it, let alone shoot. Gel sits on a bridge and disappears when the bridge does.

sections.name: Excursion Funnel
sections.card: Weightless travel along the beam. If it is carrying you the wrong way, look for the button that reverses it before assuming the route is shut. It passes through portals, so it can cross the whole chamber, and it ferries gel and cubes as well as you.

sections.name: Thermal Discouragement Beam
sections.card: The laser exists to feed receptacles and relays; the exit usually will not open until it reaches one. A redirection cube aims it freely, portals only along fixed directions, and it goes straight through glass. Held on a turret, it cooks it.

sections.name: Wheatley
sections.card: He strips the portal surfaces, shields himself and throws bombs. Let a bomb break the conversion gel pipe, paint a wall with what spills, and portal his own bombs back into him. Every stun buys time to attach one corrupted core; three of them force the transfer.

sections.name: Co-op portals and pinging
sections.card: Two players, two guns, four portals — and a portal one of you places links with the other's, which is the whole puzzle most of the time. Ping to point at a spot or to count down a timed jump; it carries without voice chat. Dying costs nothing but seconds.

sections.name: Co-op courses
sections.card: Five courses unlock in order — Team Building, then Mass and Velocity, Hard-Light Surfaces, Excursion Funnels and Mobility Gels — each teaching one mechanic before combining them. Art Therapy is the DLC course after those.

sections.name: Gravity Gun
sections.card: Secondary pulls and holds, primary punts. Explosive barrels hit hardest, sawblades cut zombies apart, and a held radiator works as a shield you can walk behind. It will not lift most enemies, but manhacks and scanners are fair game, and thrown grenades can go back where they came from.

sections.name: Ravenholm
sections.card: Ammo is scarce on purpose, so fight with the town instead of your guns. Levers drop car traps and reset them; waist-high blade traps shred zombies while you duck under; propane spray ignites from a single shot. Poison zombies switch traps off, so deal with those first. Loose blades are gravity gun ammunition.

sections.name: Strider
sections.card: RPG only, and roughly seven rockets on Normal. The rocket stays laser-guided the whole flight, so steer it wide and bring it in off-axis rather than straight up the barrel. Its warp cannon does splash damage, so keep moving between shots. A crate of rockets nearby means the fight is a long one.

sections.name: Rocket-Propelled Grenade Launcher
sections.card: Three rockets carried, and every one is steerable — hold the laser where you want it and the rocket follows, even turning right around after a miss. A gunship shoots rockets out of the air, so loop yours around behind it instead of flying it in straight.

sections.name: Antlions and the sand
sections.card: Antlions are blind and hunt vibration, so on the coast the rocks are safe and the sand is not — step off and they come up. Once you have the pheropod from the Antlion Guard it reverses: throw it and they read you as a guard and swarm whatever you marked.

sections.name: Sandtraps
sections.card: The coastal chapter that teaches the sand. Rock to rock on the way out; after the Antlion Guard you keep the pheropod and use antlions to break the Combine bunkers guarding the road to Nova Prospekt.

sections.name: Hunter-Chopper (helicopter)
sections.card: Fought from the airboat once its gun is mounted. Hold fire on it and pieces break away until it goes down. It drops contact mines and charges a pulse turret between passes; nearly dead, it makes one bombing run, so steer between the lines of falling bombs rather than trying to outrun them.

sections.name: Combine soldiers
sections.card: They move in squads of four to six and will flank you while the rest lay down covering fire, so holding one angle gets you surrounded. A grenade breaks them out of cover and into the open — and you can throw theirs back. Kill the shotgun one first and keep your distance from the rest; up close they club you.

sections.name: The Witch
sections.card: She ignores gunfire that is not aimed at her and ignores other infected; what wakes her is a flashlight or a survivor standing too close. The growl is a warning — back off and she settles. Keep coming and she stands, flails, then charges and incapacitates whoever she picked in one hit. Fire kills her in about fifteen seconds and slows her down, but only once she is already startled: light a wandering witch while she is still calm and she keeps full speed. Either way she switches to whoever burned her, not whoever woke her.

sections.name: Charger
sections.card: Shoving does nothing to him — only explosives stumble him. Treat the charge like a bull: once he commits he cannot steer, so step aside and let him hit a wall. The damage is not the problem, the destination is; near water, a ledge, or a bunched-up team he flings everybody. AI chargers take about two thirds less damage while charging, so wait until he stops rather than emptying a magazine into the run.

sections.name: Hunter
sections.card: He goes for whoever is on their own, and a long pounce does damage before the clawing starts. There is about a second to shove him out of the air, which is more warning than the jockey gives, and he has very little health once you land shots. A pounce does not end on its own — a teammate has to shove him off — so the real counter is not being the survivor at the back.

sections.name: Smoker
sections.card: The cough and the drifting green trails say he has spawned; the tongue says where. Follow it back and shoot: while he is dragging someone he stands still and takes extra damage in campaign, so one headshot ends it. If the tongue pulls the victim against an obstacle it starts choking them, so cut it fast rather than trading shots at range.

sections.name: Jockey
sections.card: The laugh is the warning. Do not swing at him mid-leap — he is much harder to hit than a hunter — step backwards as he jumps and he sails past, then shove and kill him. His damage is slow; the danger is where he steers you, which is into a witch, into acid, into a tank you were not ready for, or off a ledge.

sections.name: Boomer
sections.card: The vomit is not damage, it is a horde sent to you, and killing him at close range coats you anyway because he bursts. Shove first, then shoot. On Easy and Normal there is a second or so of warning; on Advanced and Expert he pukes on sight and backing away does not beat the arc. Being biled makes you glow to both teams, and the burst stumbles anything nearby — chargers and tanks included.

sections.name: Spitter
sections.card: The green puddle burns worse the longer it has been down, and one spit can take most of a survivor's health. Moving out of it is always right, even onto worse ground — including when you are picking someone up, because reviving means standing in it. This is why a jockey ride or a charger pin over acid is lethal rather than annoying.

sections.name: The Director
sections.card: Nothing about the spawns is fixed. Hordes of ten to thirty commons come at you every one to four minutes, from behind or off to the side, while tanks and witches only appear at threat spots the map author placed. After a heavy fight it goes quiet for roughly thirty to forty-five seconds — that pause is the healing window, and moving on ends it early. If the idle commons have thinned out, it is making room for something.

sections.name: Going down and black and white
sections.card: Going down leaves you with 300 temporary health draining three at a time until somebody picks you up. Go down a second time without healing and the screen turns grey with a heartbeat: the third one kills, and only a first aid kit clears it — pills and adrenaline do not. Death is still recoverable, by defibrillator, by reaching the safe room, or from a rescue closet, but Realism switches the closets off.

sections.name: Bile bomb
sections.card: Crowd control, not a weapon. Wherever the jar lands pulls the horde for about twenty seconds, and any infected caught in it gets attacked by its own side. Throw it well away from the team before starting a crescendo, or to buy a route past a tank — not at whatever is closest.

sections.name: Expert and Realism
sections.card: Two different kinds of hard. On Expert a single common does 20 a hit, standing still gets you killed, and a tank punch incapacitates outright. Realism is a separate switch that works on any difficulty: no outlines around your teammates, no item glow, no rescue closets, and commons shrug off body shots, so it is headshots, melee, or the magnum. Learn a map with Realism off first — the director puts supplies off the obvious path.

sections.name: Playing as the Tank
sections.card: Save him for ground that suits him: mounted guns shred you, so go around rather than through, and wait for the rest of the infected team to be up before you commit. Rocks are for the places they must walk through. Chase the panicking one or the biled one rather than the nearest one, and if a teammate has someone pinned, put your body between that survivor and their friends — the bullets hitting you are bullets not saving them. Someone running at you with a revved chainsaw gets punched before they arrive.

sections.name: Playing as the Hunter
sections.card: Pounce damage scales with distance — up to 25 on a long one — so height and a run-up matter more than surprise alone. Take the straggler, never the group, and if you have to be near the group, move like a common: the melee claw reads as horde damage until someone checks. In Left 4 Dead 2 the pounce recharges fast, so holding crouch and re-pouncing keeps pressure on.

sections.name: Playing as the Jockey
sections.card: The ride is the weapon. Steer towards a witch, a spitter pool, a fire, a ledge or an unfinished tank fight — anywhere the survivor's own team makes things worse. Rides last longer where the map turns: corners, alleys, stairwells. Off a ledge is only worth it when nobody is close enough to pick them back up, otherwise a charger does that job better.

sections.name: Playing as the Smoker
sections.card: Patience, then elevation. Wait until the team is busy, then take someone from above — a drop adds fall damage on top of the 3 a second the tongue does, and a hanging victim is far harder to rescue than one dragged along the floor. Pull towards a witch, a fire, or a drop rather than towards yourself; you have no cover. Keep moving, because standing still leaves a green cloud that marks you.

sections.name: Playing as the Charger
sections.card: Angle beats timing. A hallway lets you bowl the whole team at once; open ground lets you carry one of them far enough that the rescue costs the others real time. A drop or a hazard on the line turns the charge into a kill outright. Check nothing solid is between you and the target — hitting it stops you dead — and do not spawn early, because the grunting gives away the ambush.

sections.name: Playing as the Boomer
sections.card: Support, not damage. Set up out of sight, let them walk into range rather than charging in, and spawn just before you puke so the noise does not give you away. Bile on a grouped, distracted team while your teammates are ready is worth more than bile on whoever is nearest. Exploding on purpose in the middle of the mess is a legitimate second use.

sections.name: Playing as the Spitter
sections.card: Put the acid where they have to walk — a doorway, an alley, the stairs off a ledge — not in open ground they can step around. Spit from a balcony or a dark corner, since a headshot usually kills you outright and the glow gives you away in the light. Best paired with the horde: near a car alarm or a crowd, the pool is what stops them dealing with either.

sections.name: Sandevistan
sections.card: An operating system rather than one more implant, and it is built around blades — it slows time on demand, and some variants add crit chance and crit damage on top. Mods extend the duration or shorten the cooldown. Since patch 2.0 you can switch it off early by pressing the button again instead of burning the tail of it.

sections.name: Berserk
sections.card: The other operating system, and the melee one that does not care about time. While it runs it cuts damage taken and will not let your health fall below a quarter, and afterwards every enemy you put down returns a quarter of your maximum health. What it does for your melee weapons depends on the model installed.

sections.name: Kerenzikov
sections.card: Lets you fire while sliding, dodging or dashing, and aiming during any of those slows time for a couple of seconds. It has its own cooldown, so treat it as a repositioning tool rather than something to lean on.

sections.name: Street Cred
sections.card: A separate track from your character level, paid out by fixers for gigs, and how you finish a job changes the payout rather than just finishing it. It buys a permanent vendor discount up to 15% and unlocks better cars on the Autofixer; the good gear starts appearing around Street Cred 40, and it caps at 50.

sections.name: Lifepath
sections.card: Nomad, Streetkid or Corpo. What it changes is the opening chapter, one unique side job, and dialogue options that keep turning up later on — so pick the opening you want to play rather than the one that sounds strongest.

sections.name: Muscle
sections.card: Built at a gym or by running, cycling and swimming — fourteen seconds on the treadmill or bike is one percent, and a weights rep is one percent. It raises melee damage, respect and sex appeal, but do not max it: at 100% it works against sex appeal and some girlfriends will not talk to you. All fifty oysters, expensive clothes and a good car offset that.

sections.name: Stamina
sections.card: Endurance for sprinting, swimming and cycling; low stamina means you stop running almost immediately. It goes up with the activity itself — five percent per two and a half minutes of swimming, or per five minutes of running or biking — and four percent per fourteen seconds on gym cardio. Finishing the Burglary side missions, ten thousand dollars of stolen goods, grants unlimited stamina regardless of the stat.

sections.name: Fat
sections.card: Goes up with food, including meals on dates, and down with exercise or with not eating. Overweight slows you down and costs health, jumping and speed. Zero fat is worse: once there is nothing left to burn you start losing muscle, and after that health, so eat when the hunger warning appears.

sections.name: Respect
sections.card: Sets how many gang members you can recruit, from one up to seven. It comes from missions, killing rival gang members and police, taking territory and spraying over tags, and appearance nudges it — hair, tattoos, clothes, muscle, and wearing green in Grove Street territory most of all. It falls if you wear the wrong colours at home, kill your own, or lose turf.

sections.name: Weapon skill
sections.card: Each weapon type levels separately by hitting people and vehicles: Poor, then Gangster, then Hitman. Higher skill means better accuracy, more range, faster strafing and fire rate, and the ability to move while shooting. At Hitman the pistol, sawn-off, Tec-9 and Micro SMG can be dual wielded. Thrown weapons, melee, rifles and heavy weapons have no skill meter at all.

sections.name: Gang territory
sections.card: Opens up after Sweet's mission Doberman, and goes away for a stretch in the middle of the story before coming back. Holding turf pays: money accumulates and is collected outside the Johnson house on Grove Street, respect goes up, and rival gang members stop spawning in the streets you own.

sections.name: Girlfriends
sections.card: Six of them, and only Millie is actually required for full completion — the rest are optional. Denise and Millie arrive through story missions; Michelle, Katie and Helena become available once Flint County, Whetstone and San Fierro are open, and Barbara once Tierra Robada, Bone County and Las Venturas are. Sex appeal decides whether they will talk to you at all, and all fifty oysters covers most of that.

sections.name: Lung capacity and oysters
sections.card: How long you last underwater. It grows with time spent under, and collecting oysters is the fast way — there are fifty, along shorelines, under bridges and in pools. Let the oxygen meter empty and you lose health quickly, and surfacing gives the air back but not the health. One mission, Amphibious Assault, will not start below five percent lung capacity.

sections.name: Horseshoes
sections.card: Fifty of them around Las Venturas, and all fifty are required for 100% completion. Each one is a hundred dollars and twenty points of luck, a stat that starts at zero and only ever goes up; the full set maxes it at 1,000.

sections.name: Settlement happiness
sections.card: Happiness is just whether needs are met: food, water, beds and defense each have to be at least the number of settlers. Power is not part of it, though better machines need it. Higher happiness makes settlers more productive, and a settlement left very unhappy can be lost outright after a failed Minutemen radiant quest.

sections.name: Settlement defense and attacks
sections.card: One unit of defense per settler is the number to hit, and only workshop-built defenses count — mines do not, though they still kill attackers if you are there. Attack chance rises with stored food and water and falls with population and defense, but never below 2%; a settlement with nobody living in it is never attacked. Turn up in person and it is a normal fight with your turrets and companions helping; skip it and the game rolls defense rating plus population against the raid, which is why spreading defense thin costs you inventory and temporary happiness rather than nothing.

sections.name: SPECIAL points
sections.card: You start with one in everything and 21 to spend, so 28 in total — much less than earlier Fallouts. It is not a permanent ceiling: bobbleheads and magazines raise attributes, and each level-up lets you put the point into a SPECIAL stat instead of a perk. Your SPECIAL values are what decide which perks you can take at all.

sections.name: Perks
sections.card: The perk chart replaced skills. Every level gives one point, and it buys either a rank of a perk or a rank of the SPECIAL attribute that unlocks deeper perks in that column. Magazines scattered around the world grant extra perks that cost no points at all, and they are listed separately on the Pip-Boy.

sections.name: Power armor and fusion cores
sections.card: The frame runs on a fusion core that drains with time and faster with anything that spends AP — sprinting, V.A.T.S. When it empties you can still walk, but you are over-encumbered and lose V.A.T.S. and steady aim. No training perk is needed. Wearing it overrides your normal armour bonuses entirely and can push Strength past the usual limit of 10.

sections.name: Upgrading power armor
sections.card: Repairs and mods happen at a power armor station, and one can be built at a settlement. Upgrading a piece costs the same materials whichever tier you come from, so it is usually worth waiting until Armorer and Science are ranked up rather than paying twice — especially for the later models, whose materials are rare.

sections.name: Mirelurk queen
sections.card: Much bigger and much harder than the rest, doing heavy physical and radiation damage, and her arrival is announced by a roar. On top of the claws she spits acid that keeps damaging you after it lands, and she periodically fires a barrage of eggs that hatch into a wave of small ones — the game treats that as a grenade, so the grenade warning icon is the cue to move.

sections.name: Crafting and junk
sections.card: Almost nothing needs a schematic; the recipes are known by default. What you need is components, which come from scrapping junk at a crafting table, from scrapping world objects such as trees and cars inside a settlement you own, or from merchants. Components are drawn either from your own inventory or from the workshop of the settlement you are standing in.

genre_patterns.card: Soulslike basics: learn dodge timing, stamina management, and safe heal windows. Summon allies when available; upgrade vigor before glass-cannon damage.
